extracted.intended_audience: readers and researchers of folklore, ethnography, and cultural history (folklorists, anthropologists, historians, general educated readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A descriptive, cross-cultural account of traditional uses, placements, and ritual conditions for horses' heads and horse-shoes as talismans (protective or offensive), including associated practices for animal and household protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horses' head spite-stake (offensive talisman)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fastening a horse's head to a pole (mouth propped open) and turning its gaping jaws toward the direction whence an enemy is likely to come, in order to cast over him an evil spell (a 'spite-stake' or 'nithing-post').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used historically as an offensive magical device; direction matters (point toward enemy). Example: Eigil fixing a horse's head on a stake and invoking a curse. Later the same device was adapted as a protective talisman in other contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horses' heads on gables/poles as protective talismans
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing carved wooden representations or actual horses' heads on house gables or upon poles near stables as safeguards against evil, epidemics among animals, vermin, wolves, robbers, and spirits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When directed outwards the heads are thought to ward off evil (principle akin to the spite-stake); when displayed on gables they may also be an act of homage invoking divine blessing. Examples: Mecklenburg and Holstein carved heads on gables; hung on poles to ward off epizootics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horse skulls and parts used in household/medical remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Using parts of horses (skulls, fore-parts) in close-contact remedies and domestic cures: placed beneath pillows as febrifuges, under beds for fevers, buried beneath corner-stones for good luck, or used in baths and rainwater for certain spinal or other afflictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific recipes and frequencies may be prescribed (e.g., bathing a patient in rain-water in which a horse's head has been dipped thrice daily for three successive Thursdays). Practices vary regionally; considered folk-medicine rather than formal medicine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horse sacrifice offerings on trees (ritual deposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hanging or fastening horses' heads or bodies on trees as sacrificial offerings to deities, often as tribute or as a protection-invoking rite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direction of the head on the tree could indicate whether offering was to a good or evil deity (Altai observation). Historical example: Romans' horses' heads found fastened to trees after Varus's defeat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placing a horse's head in cribs/mangers to avert supernatural riding
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting a horse's head in the crib or manger to prevent horses from being ridden by nocturnal witches or the 'Night Hag'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recorded among the Wends in the fifteenth century; used specifically to prevent supernatural interference with animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tripartite household talismans (gable/entrance/threshold set)
rubrics_metrics.description: A traditional belief that every dwelling was protected by three emblems: (1) a horse's head on the gable, (2) a broom by the entrance as a preservative against lightning, and (3) a horse-shoe on the threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributed to Professor Christian Petersen's summary of pagan protective customs. This is a structured combinatory practice: combining different talismans for different protective functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horse-shoe as the primary anti-witch charm
rubrics_metrics.description: The horse-shoe is widely used as the anti-witch charm par excellence and a general symbol of good luck, most commonly nailed over entrance doors or on stables to prevent witches, evil spirits, and misfortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used across many regions and contexts (houses, stables, ships). Often paired with other charms (broom above the manger, sprig of rowan). Practical anecdotes show perceived efficacy (e.g., person recovered after shoe was nailed to door).

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement at the outer entrance (threshold) for maximal efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Horse-shoes are customarily placed at the outside entrance or above the principal door because an old belief holds that witches and evil spirits cannot successfully practice their craft in the open air; once inside, amulets lose much of their power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing the shoe outside is preferred; inside placement is seen as less effective but still a luck-emblem. The threshold is treated as a sacred/protective line in many cultures, reinforcing the outer placement practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation of the horse-shoe (prongs up/down/in/out) influences effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural rules prescribe the orientation of the shoe: in many places the prongs (points) must be directed so as to keep luck in (often upward) or to ward off evil (variously inward/outward). Reversing the shoe can be believed to spill luck or bring misfortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regional variation: Germany—prongs directed outward (protection), reversed brings misfortune; Oxfordshire—often placed with prongs downward; eastern Pennsylvania—prongs inward to 'spill' luck into the house; Derbyshire—prongs upward between flagstones so luck cannot spill out. Some suggest keeping one shoe both ways as hedge. Orientation is a salient practical rule and folk diagnostic when misfortune occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of nails / nail-holes as an index of luck or divination
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that the luck associated with a found horse-shoe depends on the number of nails remaining in it; more nails equal more luck. In some locales free nail-holes are counted as indicators (e.g., years until marriage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Northumberland—counting free holes to predict marriage timing; general aphorism: 'the more nails the more luck'; northern Portugal—preference for mule-shoes with an uneven number of nail-holes to counter witches ('Bruxas').

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions of forging as a quality requirement (who/when forges the shoe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some traditions require that a protective horse-shoe be forged under specific social and temporal conditions—e.g., by a bachelor of wholesome life and good character, on Saint John's Eve—to be efficacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thuringian practice: a valid talismanic shoe must have been forged by a bachelor of wholesome life on Saint John's Eve. This prescribes both the maker's status and a ritual date as part of the talisman's validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sailors' practice: nailing horse-shoes to ships' masts
rubrics_metrics.description: Sailors nail horse-shoes to the mast or other parts of a vessel as protection at sea, analogous to household usage on land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mariners sometimes prize a shoe of a 'wraith-horse' as especially potent. The shoe is used on fishing boats and large sea-going craft alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horse-shoe as prevention/trap against witches and nightmare
rubrics_metrics.description: Horse-shoes are nailed to byre-doors and bedroom doors as safeguards: to prevent witches from riding horses, drawing milk, entering houses, and to avert nightmares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include stabilizing cattle health (first shoe on a stallion hung on byre protects cows) and placing an old horse-shoe above the bedroom door to prevent nightmare. Practical rituals (nailing, tying) accompany belief-based assertions of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-patterns: counterfeit or inappropriate amulets fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting inappropriate items (e.g., donkey-shoes for horse-shoes) or incorrect placement/orientation undermines or nullifies the talisman's protective power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: a carpenter had donkeys' shoes substituted and the supposed witch then could cross the threshold. This functions as a folk diagnostic/explanation for talisman failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of charms (broom, rowan sprig, red thread) for animal protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of multiple protective objects together—e.g., broom above the manger, sprigs of rowan tied with red thread to cows' tails, horse-shoes on thresholds—to protect animals and households from witches and mischief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scottish practice: tie rowan sprigs with red thread to the cow's tail; hang broom above manger; nail horse-shoe to byre-door. Combined measures are depicted as the 'adequate protection' against specific folk malefactions like milk-stealing by witches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of horse parts to protect hives and livestock
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing skulls or other horse parts near beehives, in pigsties, or about sheepfolds to protect bees and animals from witchcraft, the 'evil eye', wolves, and other harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tartars hanging skulls or feet near hives; Kalmuks placing horse heads and hides on scaffolds; Transylvanian and Magyar shepherds fixing skulls to palings or burying beneath floors for protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of talismans in liminal/sacred locations (thresholds, between houses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic placement of charms in liminal zones—thresholds, doorways, between quarrelsome neighbors' houses, between flagstones—because such places are seen as lines separating domestic safety from external danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thresholds function as household altars in folk belief; thus amulets placed there are believed to mediate entry of spirits. Example: placing a shoe between quarrelsome houses to prevent mutual harm; driving a shoe between two flagstones near the door in Derbyshire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of inscriptions and other symbolic talismans above doors
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing religious or protective inscriptions (Biblical verses, prayers, exhortations) over entrances as talismanic devices, sometimes serving analogous functions to the horse-shoe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Swiss and Italian house inscriptions invoking divine protection, or sentences committing the house to Fortune; such inscriptions can complement or substitute for physical amulets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ritual timing and festival associations (St. John's Day uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain talismanic acts are tied to calendrical rituals or festivals, such as burying broken horse-shoes under trees or placing them in animal troughs on St. John's Day for seasonal protection or healing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Transylvanian peasants place broken horse-shoes in animals' drinking-troughs on St. John's Day; in Lincolnshire, burying horse-shoes under ash-trees to 'charm' them. Timing and festival association are presented as part of the efficacy conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use among itinerant/ethnic groups for site- and corpse-protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Gypsy/Transylvanian practices of hanging/burying skulls at palings, under floors, and on graves to prevent witches and protect dwellings and burial sites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recorded practices: gypsies fasten skulls to fence-palings, bury them beneath earth-cavern floors, or fix talismans on graves to ensure sacred ground is not trodden by witches. These are community-specific adaptations of broader talismanic logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horse-staffs and shamanic paraphernalia carved as horses' heads
rubrics_metrics.description: Magico-religious practitioners (shamans, wizards) carry staves topped with carved horses' heads and wear robes decorated with fetiches (bells, iron) as part of ritual expertise and spirit-control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in ceremonies to 'assist' in sorcery (e.g., shamans who use staves to leap). Inclusion of horse-head carvings on ritual paraphernalia signals the animal's central symbolic potency in magical systems.
